    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34895v1</id>
    <title>Schrödinger's Legacy: The Wave Function and Quantum Reality</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:48:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34895v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34895v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The article discusses how Schrödinger arrived at the formulation of wave mechanics and his legacy on the philosophy of quantum mechanics, focusing in particular on the metaphysics of the wave function. Schrödinger's interpretation of the wave function as electron charge density is generally dismissed or presented only as a curious historical example in the literature. On a closer look, however, while this interpretation was eventually abandoned in favor of Born's statistical interpretation, Schrödinger's idea survived in modern realist approaches to the wave function, such as the mass-density approach and the multi-field interpretation. It also proved to be of great utility in modern techniques and approximations in quantum chemistry to compute the shape of atoms and molecules. Overall, Schrödinger's interpretation of the wave function and his realist understanding of quantum mechanics paved the way to modern attempts to define a clear ontology of the microscopic world, a tradition that survived the Copenhagen interpretation of Bohr and Heisenberg and that is still present today.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34894v1</id>
    <title>What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:47:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34894v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34894v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/ρ$, and its yield stress $σ_Y/ρ$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.</summary>

    <title>Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:47:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34891v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34891v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Qubit loss is a significant source of error in many quantum hardware platforms, requiring circuits that periodically replace or reset qubits to maintain fault-tolerance. When the reset process includes loss-resolving measurements, this information can improve decoding and substantially reduce overhead compared to the case where this information is not available. Prior work has demonstrated loss-tolerant circuits for the surface code that show significantly improved thresholds and subthreshold scaling by incorporating loss information. However, the computational complexity of loss simulation and decoding, which falls outside of the usual stabilizer framework, has limited extending these studies to high-rate qLDPC codes, which are already challenging to decode in the absence of loss. In this work, we present a loss-aware convolutional neural-network (CNN) decoder framework that circumvents this challenge. Training is enabled by a novel sampler, \texttt{slim}, which achieves a throughput for circuits with Pauli noise and loss that is comparable to the state-of-the-art for pure Pauli noise. On the surface code with loss, the decoder matches the accuracy of computationally expensive most-likely error (MLE) decoders at much lower latency. This demonstrates that loss-dominated error models can also significantly improve performance in a high-rate qLDPC code, and provides a simulation and decoder training platform that can be extended to other codes and algorithmic gadgets.</summary>

    <title>The Price of Quantum Advantage in Computational Chemistry</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:45:50Z</updated>

    <summary>As the fault-tolerant era approaches, the question shifts from ``is it possible'' to ``is it worthwhile.'' To assess practical quantum advantage against reliable classical baselines, we examine 26 benchmark instances including FeMoco, iron-sulfur clusters, cytochrome P450, and ruthenium catalysts using two selected configuration interaction solvers, SHCI and TrimCI. Comparing classical workloads with fault-tolerant resource estimates, we calculate the break-even whole-QPU hourly price. Wavefunction analysis further reveals how orbital choice affects the determinant support required for target-state overlap in quantum phase estimation (QPE).     <title>Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:45:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34887v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34887v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. First, we propose a hybrid tree architecture that integrates both feature-based and case-based splits, allowing for heterogeneous splits throughout the tree. Second, we introduce a novel type of split that leverages a selective case-based approach: when a split is needed, our method searches for the most informative subset of features to define the split, effectively balancing the specificity of case-based methods with the simplicity of feature-based ones. Experiments on a diverse set of tabular datasets show that our method outperforms standard decision trees and achieves performance on par with ensemble methods, while producing shallow trees that retain or even improve predictive accuracy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34881v1</id>
    <title>Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:39:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34881v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34881v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.</summary>

    <title>How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:37:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34875v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34875v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34874v1</id>
    <title>Exact monogamy of steering and remote Wigner negativity for multimode Gaussian nodes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:36:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34874v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34874v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Optical quantum networks route correlations through nodes that hold several modes and are linked to many neighbors. Steering is the correlation behind one-sided device-independent tasks and behind the remote preparation of non-Gaussian states. It is monogamous for a single mode, which can be steered by only one party, but how many neighbors can steer a node with $k$ modes was not known. We show that for Gaussian states the answer is exactly $2k-1$ when the neighbors use Gaussian measurements, with any number of measurement settings. The limit follows from a simple bound. To every neighbor we assign a share, computed from the covariance matrix, and we prove that the shares of all neighbors add up to at most $k$, irrespective of the amount of squeezing, amplification or noise the network contains. A neighbor steers the node by Gaussian measurements exactly when its share exceeds one half, and a network built from a harmonic tight frame reaches the limit. The same number governs remote Wigner negativity. A heralded non-Gaussian operation at the node can make at most $2k-1$ neighbors Wigner negative, and in our network a single heralded projection makes all of them negative in the same run. With $n$ settings of arbitrary measurements, at most $nk-1$ neighbors can steer the node or violate a Bell inequality with it. More than $2k-1$ neighbors can therefore steer the node or violate a Bell inequality with it only if they use non-Gaussian measurements with at least three settings, whereas entanglement can reach any number of neighbors. These results determine exactly how many neighbors one multimode node can serve with steering and with remote Wigner negativity.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-25T18:35:01Z</updated>

    <summary>Magic captures nonstabilizerness, a resource required for quantum computational speedups. We prove the existence of multi-qubit nonstabilizer states from which no pure magic can be distilled, even with arbitrarily many copies and rounds of stabilizer operations. Such bound magic states have previously been only known to exist in odd Hilbert-space dimensions, where positivity of discrete Wigner functions can be used analogously to the positive partial transpose (PPT) criterion for bound entanglement. We introduce a PPT analogue for magic in multi-qubit systems that is closed under tensor products and stabilizer operations and reduces to the stabilizer polytope for one and two qubits. This enables the proof of multi-qubit bound magic and the explicit construction of bound magic states for $n \geq 3$ qubits.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-25T18:34:47Z</updated>

    <title>Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation</title>

    <summary>Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions.     <title>State convertibility in quantum-state texture from a general form of free operations</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:30:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34865v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34865v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>State convertibility specifies which transformations between states a quantum resource theory allows. In quantum-state texture, deterministic conversion criteria are known for qubits and pure sources in arbitrary dimension, but a general criterion for mixed states in higher dimensions is missing. We derive this exact criterion from a complete characterization of free operations in arbitrary finite dimension. Because the unique free state is pure, every free operation splits into a quantum filter and a residual completely positive map. Using this decomposition, we show that every allowed conversion admits a two-outcome measurement that retains the filtered state after one outcome and prepares a fixed state after the other. Conversion thus reduces to finding such a filter whose unnormalized output leaves a positive semidefinite remainder when subtracted from the target, a search we show to be solvable by semidefinite programming. Beyond deterministic conversion, the characterization of free operations can be used to study probabilistic and assisted manipulation of quantum-state texture. More broadly, since the construction relies on a pure fixed state, it also applies to other resource theories defined by free operations fixing such a state.</summary>

    <summary>Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv</summary>

    <title>BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:29:36Z</updated>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34862v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34859v1</id>
    <title>Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Technical Validation of Re-identification Tests under the EDPB Anonymisation Guidelines</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:28:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34859v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34859v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), published for consultation in July 2026, assess anonymity relative to the entities that may access data. They bring AI models into scope and call for testing, but do not say how a re-identification test should be designed or validated, or how far its result counts as evidence. Building on our reply to the consultation, we describe a framework based on a secure processing environment whose outputs are reviewed before release (an airlock), and distinguish forms of release and three types of evidence: formal, empirical and indirect. We raise seven open questions, each with a scenario, and examine their technical side in three settings: the release of model weights (the trained parameters of a machine learning model), review at an airlock, and regulatory sandboxes, in which an authority supervises development and testing. In each setting the assessment depends on how far a test result can be relied on, since a failed re-identification attempt may mean only that the test was too weak. Drawing on measurement practice in other regulated fields, we call for re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods, with stated detection limit, bias and uncertainty.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34858v1</id>
    <title>From Prediction to Decision: Decision-Focused Fine-Tuning of Autoregressive Tabular Transformers for Cost-Sensitive Financial Events</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:27:48Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34858v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34858v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Autoregressive transformers trained on tokenized tabular event streams are a simple and strong baseline for predicting financial events such as fraud. Yet institutions do not act on probabilities; they act on decisions whose consequences are asymmetric and heteroscedastic: the cost of a missed high-value fraud and that of a wrongly declined small purchase are not the same. The standard bridge is post-hoc Bayes-optimal thresholding of calibrated probabilities under a cost matrix. We ask whether fine-tuning the model to the decision objective can do better. We fine-tune the same pretrained model so that its restricted softmax over label tokens (already a distribution over business actions) maximizes expected utility under an institution-specified, amount-scaled cost matrix. Because the reward is a known function of (action, outcome, amount) and the outcome is observed in the data, the expected-utility objective and its gradient are available in closed form. This is example-dependent cost-sensitive learning whose per-example loss is linear in the predicted probability, with no sampling, critics, or advantage estimation. A KL anchor to the pretrained model and an auxiliary language-modeling term preserve calibration and the generative event model. A sampled, group-normalized (GRPO-style) variant provides the extension point to trajectory-level rewards.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34853v1</id>
    <title>Monotonic probes of asymmetry and robustness of the quantum Mpemba effect</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:25:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34853v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34853v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Entanglement asymmetry has emerged as a powerful probe of symmetry restoration and the quantum Mpemba effect. However, its conventional Rényi generalizations, defined as differences of Rényi entropies, are not monotones in the resource-theoretic sense. Here, we investigate an alternative family of asymmetry quantifiers based on sandwiched Rényi divergences, which satisfy monotonicity under symmetry-preserving quantum channels. Developing a two-parameter replica approach, we show how these quantities can be computed from charged moments and establish a remarkable correspondence with conventional Rényi asymmetries under the inversion of the Rényi index, $α\leftrightarrow 1/α$. This relation, exact for pure states, holds at leading order in the relevant scaling limits for homogeneous quantum quenches, including interacting integrable systems, and for Haar-random states. Applying these results to quenches from tilted ferromagnetic states, we demonstrate that the quantum Mpemba effect is remarkably robust, occurring throughout the entire family of sandwiched Rényi asymmetry monotones. We identify dynamical regimes in quenches from spatially inhomogeneous initial states where conventional Rényi asymmetries and genuine monotones exhibit qualitatively different behaviours. We also investigate a solvable toy model illustrating the possible dependence of Mpemba crossings on the Rényi index. Our findings establish a connection between conventional Rényi asymmetries and quantum resource theory, explaining their effectiveness in broad classes of nonequilibrium protocols while highlighting the additional information provided by genuine asymmetry monotones.</summary>

    <title>DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:25:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34852v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34852v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34848v1</id>
    <title>Put the World Back: Timestamps Matter in Time Series Reasoning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:23:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34848v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34848v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to time series reasoning. However, current evaluations often give models events in chronological order and already matched to the time series. This makes it unclear whether models use timestamps to connect events with observations or simply take shortcuts. To expose this ambiguity, we reformulate time series reasoning from a world-to-series projection perspective, viewing timestamps as explicit indices that connect numerical observations and external events to shared world states. We identify three structures that timestamps can make explicit: temporal causal structure, time semantics, and event-series alignment. Building on this perspective, we develop a diagnostic protocol that distinguishes timestamp-grounded reasoning from correlational shortcuts, a distinction that accuracy-based benchmarks cannot make. Controlled interventions on 310 questions from two tasks show that high accuracy can persist when timestamps are replaced by relative offsets or removed, while breaking event-series alignment induces systematic failures. When context is pre-aligned, models barely need timestamps. When order is missing, they use dates to recall world knowledge. Without dates, they rely on correlational shortcuts and rarely notice incorrect timestamps. These findings show that high accuracy on pre-aligned, ordered inputs does not establish that a model uses timestamps to synchronize observations with the world. We release our code, model outputs, and trajectory labels at https://github.com/tingrui-huang/timestamps-matter.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34843v1</id>
    <title>Probing Visual Idiosyncrasies in Text-to-Image Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:20:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34843v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34843v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Text-to-Image (T2I) models turn short text descriptions into images, and the leading models now produce images of comparable visual quality. Whether their outputs still carry model-specific characteristics matters for attribution, for model comparison beyond aggregate quality, and for evaluations that assume anonymity. We ask whether images from frontier T2I models can still be classified by source, and which visual properties make this possible. Here we show that a standard ResNet-50 identifies the source of an image among HiDream-O1-Dev, FLUX.2-dev, HunyuanImage-3.0, and Qwen-Image-2512, the four highest-ranked open-source models on the Text-to-Image Arena, with 100.00% accuracy on held-out prompts. Human participants reach only 62.61% on the pairwise version of this task, so the distinguishing cues are not visually obvious. They are also not tied to a particular classifier and survive severe image corruptions and out-of-distribution prompts. We trace them to visual idiosyncrasies at three levels. Low-level texture statistics alone let a lightweight multi-layer perceptron match ResNet-50. Object layout, depth, and albedo estimated from the images each carry a source signal. Image captions reveal model-specific preferences in style and background that the prompts never specify. A one-sentence hint about these cues raises human accuracy by 9.03 percentage points. These idiosyncrasies make source classification a tool for measuring similarity between models and between real and generated images, and they caution against assuming anonymity in human preference evaluation of T2I models.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34841v1</id>
    <title>Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:19:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34841v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34841v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from.</summary>

    <title>Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:18:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34840v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $β\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($β>0$) and risk-seeking ($β<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|β|/(1-γ)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.</summary>

    <title>Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:12:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34831v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34831v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.</summary>

    <title>Not all world models can doubt: how training objective and architecture shape epistemic uncertainty in JEPA and RSSM world models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-25T18:11:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34830v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.34830v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>World models predict how an environment responds to actions, so that candidate actions can be evaluated before execution. Executed actions, or decisions, taken in this manner are only as reliable as the model's predictive capabilities, and predictions in turn are only reliable within the model's experience. Epistemic uncertainty (EU) is the signal that marks where that experience ends. In this work we offer an extensive empirical study on how training objectives and architectures shape epistemic uncertainty of world models. More precisely, we present a controlled comparison of post-hoc EU (last-layer Laplace and ensembles) between two dominant models of different paradigms: 1) LeWorldModel (LeWM): A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), which predicts the next embedding without a decoder, and 2) DreamerV3: A recurrent state-space model (RSSM), which reconstructs the observation from a recurrent latent state. In ten simulated visual-control environments, we follow a controlled state perturbation of the environment state through every stage of the models up to the final EU estimate. We find that the RSSM attenuates the state perturbation through two mechanisms before it reaches an estimator on the predictor feature. Its recurrent update averages over context, so a change in a single frame reaches the state at a fraction of its size and recovers only as the change persists. Its reconstruction objective weights an entity by the pixels it covers, so a small object can be lost due to the training objective. The JEPA has neither mechanism and passes the change through all stages to the uncertainty. We further show that this translates to gaps in five uncertainty related downstream tasks, from unfamiliar-state detection to uncertainty-penalised planning: the RSSM uncertainty misses deviations that its own posterior registers, whereas the JEPA uncertainty reports what its model sees.</summary>

The ancillary study is a genetic analysis of a group of candidate genes that aims to identify biomarkers for changes in visual processing. This will allow to distinguish among more homogeneous and specific groups in future studies on larger cannabis user population. * Affiliation to social security plan
* Normal visual acuity or adjusted to normal and normal dilated fundus examination
* Signature of informed consent
* Cannabis user group: More than 7 cannabis uses per week during the previous month
* Cannabis user group: Positive urinary analysis for presence of cannabis
* Healthy, non user control group: Absence of cannabis and tobacco use during last 12 months
* Healthy, non user control group: Negative urinary analysis for presence of cannabis
* Healthy, non user control group: Age and sex matching with cannabis user group
* Healthy, tobacco user control group: Tobacco use from at least 12 months
* Healthy, tobacco user control group: Low to very strong addiction to tobacco (Fagerström test)
* Healthy, tobacco user control group: Absence of cannabis use from more than 12 months
* Healthy, tobacco user control group: Negative urinary analysis for presence of cannabis
* Healthy, tobacco user control group:Age and sex matching with cannabis user group
* Schizophrenia patient control group: Schizophrenia according to DMS IV criteria (MINI test)
* Schizophrenia patient control group: Absence of cannabis use from more than one month (regardless of tobacco use)
* Schizophrenia patient control group: Negative urinary analysis for presence of cannabis
* Schizophrenia patient control group: Age and sex matching with cannabis user group

Exclusion Criteria:

* Acute psychiatric pathology (axis I of DSM IV, measured by MINI) except anxiety disorder (except schizophrenia group)
* Deficiency of the subject making difficult or impossible his/her participation to the study or the comprehension of the information
* Dyslexia
* Addiction to alcohol according to AUDIT scale
* Abuse or addiction to other substances according to DSM IV criteria
* Acute retinal disorder
* Chronic glaucoma
* Ophthalmic pathology affecting visual acuity
* Current ocular infection
* Persons under guardianship, curatorship or judicial protection
* Pregnant or breast-feeding women
* Persons with life-and-death emergency
* Absence of social security plan
* Results of preliminary medical examinations incompatible with the study

Ibrutinib may stop the growth of cancer cells by blocking some of the enzymes needed for cell growth.","detailedDescription":"PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine the overall response rate (complete response \[CR\] and partial response \[PR\]) of hairy cell leukemia (HCL) at 32 weeks after beginning therapy with single-agent ibrutinib.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To characterize the toxicity and tolerability of single-agent ibrutinib when administered to patients with HCL.

II. To characterize the progression-free (PFS) and overall survival (OS) of single-agent ibrutinib when administered to patients with HCL.

III. To determine the rate of molecular remission (minimal residual disease \[MRD\]-negative CR) among all patients, defined as resolution of all detectable disease below the limits of detection by immunohistochemistry and/or 4-color flow cytometry assay at 32 weeks after beginning ibrutinib therapy.

IV. To characterize immunologic outcomes during single agent ibrutinib administration.

V. To explore the effect of ibrutinib (PCI-32765) on traditional and new biomarkers in HCL including:

Va. Confirmation of expression BRAFV600E in leukemia cells Vb. Pharmacodynamic effects of BTK inhibition on phosphorylated (phospho) ERK regulation, as well as other potential protein kinase targets of ibrutinib (exploratory) Vc. Serum soluble IL-2 receptor correlation with response to ibrutinib therapy Vd. Documentation of and quantification of minimal residual disease following maximal response, with flow cytometric analysis and immunohistochemical stains of the bone marrow, as predictors of remission duration after ibrutinib therapy.

OUTLINE:

Patients receive ibrutinib orally (PO) once daily (QD) on days 1-28. Cycles repeat every 28 days for up to 8 cycles if lack of response to therapy, up to 12 cycles if failure to achieve an objective response (CR/PR), or continually at per physician discretion in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Additionally, patients undergo bone marrow aspiration and biopsy, blood sample collection, and computed tomography (CT) or ultrasound throughout the study.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up every 3 months."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Hairy Cell Leukemia","Hairy Cell Leukemia Variant","Recurrent Hairy Cell Leukemia","Recurrent Hairy Cell Leukemia Variant"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["PHASE2"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"NA","interventionModel":"SINGLE_GROUP","primaryPurpose":"TREATMENT","maskingInfo":{"masking":"NONE"}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":44,"type":"ESTIMATED"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"Treatment (ibrutinib)","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"Patients receive ibrutinib PO QD on days 1-28. Graphical analyses will be used as well as repeated measure models (linear or nonlinear mixed models, generalized estimating equation) to assess the PK markers in relation to clinical treatment outcomes.","timeFrame":"Predose, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 hours post-dose on days 1 and 8 of cycle 1 and predose and 2 hours on days 15 and 22 of cycle 1 and day 1 of cycle 2"}]},"eligibilityModule":{"eligibilityCriteria":"Inclusion Criteria:

* Histologically confirmed diagnosis of hairy cell leukemia or variant according to World Health Organization (WHO) criteria with any of the following indications for therapy:

  * Hemoglobin \< 11 g/dL
  * Platelet count \< 100,000/mL
  * Absolute neutrophil count \< 1,000/mL
  * Progressive or symptomatic splenomegaly or hepatomegaly
  * Enlarging lymphadenopathy \>= 2 cm
  * Absolute lymphocyte count \> 5,000/mL
  * Disease related constitutional symptoms consisting of unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight over the preceding 6 months, Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program (CTEP) active version of the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grade 2 or 3 fatigue, fevers \> 100.5 degrees Fahrenheit (F) or night sweats for greater than 2 weeks without evidence of infection
* Patients with classic hairy cell leukemia may receive therapy under the following conditions:

  * After at least 1 prior purine nucleoside analog-containing regimen (fludarabine, pentostatin, or cladribine), or
  * Relapsed or de novo disease if deemed medically unfit for therapy with a purine nucleoside analog

    * Because there is no recognized standard of care for patients with variant hairy cell leukemia, both previously treated and previously untreated patients with this diagnosis will be eligible
* Age ≥ 18 years. Because no dosing or adverse event data are currently available on the use of ibrutinib in patients \< 18 years of age, children are excluded from this study, but may be eligible for future pediatric trials
* Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status =\< 2 (Karnofsky \>= 60%)
* Life expectancy of greater than 12 months
* Creatinine =\< 2.0 mg/dL, and/or creatinine clearance (estimated glomerular filtration rate \[GFR\] \[Cockcroft-Gault\]) \>= 30 mL/min
* Total bilirubin =\< 1.5 x upper limit of normal (ULN) (unless disease related or due to Gilbert's disease)
* Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) =\< 3.0 x ULN (unless disease related)
* Prothrombin time (PT)/international normalized ratio (INR) \< 1.5 x ULN
* Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) (activated partial thromboplastin time \[aPTT\]) \< 1.5 x ULN
* Because patients with HCL are typically pancytopenic at presentation for treatment, patients will be eligible without respect to baseline peripheral blood cell counts if they otherwise meet inclusion criteria
* The effects of ibrutinib on the developing human fetus are unknown; for this reason, and because tyrosine kinase inhibitors may be teratogenic, women of child-bearing potential and men must agree to use adequate contraception (hormonal or barrier method of birth control; abstinence) prior to study entry; female patients who are of non-reproductive potential (i.e., post-menopausal by history - no menses for \>= 1 year; or history of hysterectomy; or history of bilateral tubal ligation; or history of bilateral oophorectomy); female patients of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test upon study entry; male and female patients who agree to use highly effective methods of birth control (e.g., condoms, implants, injectables, combined oral contraceptives, some intrauterine devices \[IUDs\], complete sexual abstinence, or sterilized partner) during the period of therapy and for 90 days after the last dose of study drug; should a woman become pregnant or suspect she is pregnant while she or her partner is participating in this study, she should inform her treating physician immediately
* Ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent document

Exclusion Criteria:

* Chemotherapy =\< 21 days prior to first administration of study treatment and/or monoclonal antibody =\< 6 weeks prior to first administration of study treatment
* Patients who are receiving any other investigational agents
* Patients with known brain metastases should be excluded from this clinical trial because of their poor prognosis and because they often develop progressive neurologic dysfunction that would confound the evaluation of neurologic and other adverse events
* History of allergic reactions attributed to compounds of similar chemical or biologic composition as ibrutinib
* Ibrutinib is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4/5; patients who received a strong cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A inhibitor within 7 days prior to the first dose of ibrutinib or patients who require continuous treatment with a strong CYP3A inhibitor; therefore, any medications or substances that are strong inhibitors of CYP3A4/5 should be discontinued; patients unable to change these medications must be excluded from participation; because the lists of these agents are constantly changing, it is important to regularly consult a frequently-updated list; medical reference texts such as the Physicians' Desk Reference may also provide this information; as part of the enrollment/informed consent procedures, the patient will be counseled on the risk of interactions with other agents, and what to do if new medications need to be prescribed or if the patient is considering a new over-the-counter medicine or herbal product
* Uncontrolled intercurrent illness including, but not limited to, ongoing or active infection, symptomatic congestive heart failure, unstable angina pectoris, cardiac arrhythmia, or psychiatric illness/social situations that would limit compliance with study requirements; recent infections requiring systemic treatment need to have completed therapy \> 14 days before the first dose of study drug
* Pregnant women are excluded from this study because ibrutinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor with the potential for teratogenic or abortifacient effects; because there is an unknown but potential risk for adverse events in nursing infants secondary to treatment of the mother with ibrutinib, breastfeeding should be discontinued if the mother is treated with ibrutinib
* Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-positive patients will be eligible unless they have been previously diagnosed with an acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)-defining illness
* Patients who require anticoagulation with warfarin (Coumadin) or who have taken warfarin within 28 days prior to enrollment are not eligible due to a potential increased risk of hemorrhage; patients who are currently taking vitamin K antagonists are also ineligible for this study
* Patients requiring daily corticosteroids at a prednisone equivalent of \>= 20 mg daily should not be enrolled; if corticosteroids can be discontinued (or reduced to \< 20 mg per day of prednisone or equivalent), the discontinuation or dose reduction should be done at least 7 days prior to first dose
* Prior exposure to a Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor
* Major surgery within 4 weeks of first dose of study drug
* A history of prior malignancy, with the exception of the following:

  * Malignancy treated with curative intent and with no evidence of active disease present for more than 3 years prior to screening, and felt to be at low risk for recurrence by the treating physician
  * Adequately treated non-melanomatous skin cancer or lentigo maligna melanoma without current evidence of disease
  * Adequately treated cervical carcinoma in situ without current evidence of disease
* Currently active clinically significant cardiovascular disease such as: uncontrolled arrhythmia, congestive heart failure, or class 3 or 4 congestive heart failure as defined by the New York Heart Association Functional Classification or history of myocardial infarction, unstable angina, or acute coronary syndrome within 6 months prior to first dose with study drug
* Patient is unable to swallow capsules, or has disease significantly affecting gastrointestinal function or resection of the stomach or small bowel, or symptomatic inflammatory bowel disease or ulcerative colitis, or partial or complete bowel obstruction
* History of stroke or intracranial hemorrhage within 6 months prior to enrollment
* Serologic status reflecting active hepatitis B or C infection; patients that are positive for hepatitis B core antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), or hepatitis C antibody must have a negative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) prior to enrollment; (PCR positive patients will be excluded)
* Concurrent systemic immunosuppressant therapy other than corticosteroids (e.g., cyclosporine A, tacrolimus, etc.) within 28 days of the first dose of study drug

(Phase II)

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

Researchers want to learn if FLT-PET scans can show an early response to chemotherapy.","detailedDescription":"FLT-PET Scan:

An FLT-PET scan uses the FLT solution, which contains a small amount of radioactive material, to help locate cancer cells inside the body. This scan may help doctors find solid tumors as well as learn if these tumors are growing and how fast they are growing. This information could be used to help predict if the cancer will respond to treatment.

Study Visits:

Within 2 weeks before Day 1 of Cycle 1 and between Days 19 and 21 of Cycle 1, you will have a FLT-PET scan.

For at least 4 hours before the FLT-PET scan, you must not eat or drink anything. You will receive the FLT solution by vein. The FLT solution is a mildly radioactive material. The radioactive nature of the solution allows the scanner to "see" it in certain places in your body. After the injection, you will need to rest quietly until it is time for the scan. The amount of rest time may vary, but be prepared to wait for about 60 minutes. During the scan, you will lie flat on your back on a table. After the solution is injected into a vein, the PET scanner takes pictures of the radioactive solution as it moves through the body and collects at various sites in the body. By watching how the solution travels through the body and studying where the solution collects, researchers can learn the status of disease in the body. The scan itself may last about 40-60 minutes.

Your vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, and breathing rate) will be measured before each injection of the FLT solution, 30 minutes after each injection, and before each PET scan. You will be allowed to leave 30 minutes after your scan, if your vital signs are acceptable.

Length of Study:

You will be off this study after the second FLT-PET scan. You will be taken off study early if you have intolerable side effects or the study doctor thinks it is in your best interest.

Some men who take opioid-based medications (narcotics) for pain develop low testosterone levels. Research has shown that low testosterone levels may make a person more sensitive to pain. This means that if a person with a painful condition develops low testosterone level as a result of his pain medications, he might become more sensitive to pain and so may need higher doses of pain medications for pain control.

Testosterone is a male hormone that is important for sperm production and the development of male characteristics such as muscle mass and strength, fat distribution, bone mass and sex drive. Testosterone hormone replacement therapy has been used for decades to treat men with low testosterone levels (male hypogonadism). Testosterone replacement therapies are available in the form of an injection into the muscle, implants under the skin, oral capsules taken by mouth, topical gels applied to the skin, and skin patches.

This study will use Fortesta®, a topical testosterone gel (T-gel) absorbed into the skin. Fortesta® is currently on the market as an FDA-approved treatment of male hypogonadism (low testosterone levels).

Men with non-cancer related pain who take opioid-based medications for pain and have low testosterone levels may join this study. Only couples are eligible for participation. In order to be eligible, the couple must meet each of the following criteria:

1. The patient has received a cancer diagnosis (all malignancies will be included);
2. The patient completed cancer treatment with either curative or palliative intent ≥ 3 months earlier. Patients who currently receive hormone therapy are eligible;
3. The patient experiences severe levels of fatigue (score of ≥ 35 on the Checklist Individual Strength, subscale fatigue severity (CIS-fatigue));
4. The patient has been suffering from severe fatigue for ≥ 3 months (as self-reported by the patient);
5. The patient was ≥ 18 years old at disease onset;
6. The partner is ≥ 18 years old;
7. Both couple members live together;
8. Both couple members have good command of the Dutch language (checked implicitly during registration);
9. Both couple members have adequate computer literacy and have access to an internet-connected computer, laptop or tablet (based on self-report);
10. Both couple members agree to participate in the research.

Exclusion Criteria:

The couple will be excluded in case:

1. The patient is currently following an evidence-based therapy for CCRF (i.e. Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy, mindfulness-based therapy, exercising/physiotherapy) as self-reported at the (telephone) screening;
2. The patient suffers from a condition that can explain his/her fatigue and is potentially treatable (e.g. anemia);
3. The therapist decides, based on information collected during the intake session, that the intervention is not suitable for the couple. Criteria that will be considered include, but are not limited to:

   * presence of severe psychiatric morbidity such as suicidal ideation and/or psychosis (as assessed by the therapist at the intake session). Mild depression is not an exclusion criterion. A score of ≥ 20 on the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) at T0 is considered indicative of depression. SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

To evaluate Pathological Remission Rate (pCR/MPR/PR rate), Objective Response Rate (ORR), Recurrence Free Survival (RFS) and Overall Survival (OS).

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

Analysis of liver metastasis before and after treatment to compare molecular and immunophenotypic changes.

OUTLINE:

Patients receive Sintilimab + XELOX regimen every 3 weeks for 4 cycles and Bevacizumab every 3 weeks for 2 cycles. * Normal hematological function (platelets\>90×109/L; white blood cells\>3×109/L; neutrophils\>1.5×109/L)
* Serum bilirubin ≤ 1.5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), transaminase ≤ 5 times ULN, alkaline phosphatase ≤2.5 ULN, No ascites, normal coagulation function, albumin ≥35g/L
* Child-Pugh classification of the liver is A
* Serum creatinine is less than the upper limit of normal (ULN), or the calculated creatinine clearance rate is greater than 50ml/min (using Cockcroft-Gault formula)
* ECOG score 0-1
* Life expectancy\> 3 months
* Signed and written informed consent
* Willing and able to follow up until death or the end of the study or the study is terminated

Exclusion Criteria:

* Presence of distant metastases outside the liver after the diagnosis of colorectal cancer
* Liver metastases have been treated with chemotherapy, targeted drugs, intervention, immunotherapy, radiotherapy, etc.
* No surgical resection plan for liver metastases

* Any residual toxicity from previous chemotherapy (except for hair loss), such as peripheral neuropathy ≥NCI CTC v3.0 Grade 2

* Suffering from interstitial lung disease that requires steroid therapy
* Medical history of active autoimmune disease that needs symptomatic treatment within the past 2 years. * History of primary immunodeficiency

* Known history of allergies related to organ transplantation or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
* Allergic to any monoclonal antibody or chemotherapeutic drug (fluorouracil, oxaliplatin) and its ingredients

* Patients with apparent symptoms of intestinal obstruction

* Presence of central nervous system disease ( such as primary brain tumor, history of uncontrollable epilepsy, any brain metastases or stroke)

* Received any drug treatment used for this study in the last 28 days

This part of the study will recruit 60 patients.","detailedDescription":"A multicentre phase II study to determine the safety and efficacy of EUS-guided nCLE in patients with suspected cystic tumours of the pancreas in whom endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) is clinically indicated. Patients will be recruited sequentially to undergo nCLE as part of their routine diagnostic evaluation, followed by standard surveillance. This part of the study will recruit 60 patients. The study also includes a feasibility study to evaluate the role of intraoperative nCLE in the diagnosis and staging of pancreatic tumours. This part of the study will recruit a further 20 patients.

Primary endpoint:

Assess the diagnostic performance of the Cellvizio nCLE system in the characterization of pancreatic cysts, compared to standard diagnostic modalities.

Secondary endpoints:

* Assess the safety and efficacy of EUS-nCLE.
* Assess the impact of the Cellvizio nCLE system on the management of patients with pancreatic cysts.
* Develop and validate interpretation criteria for nCLE in the pancreas.

5. Age \>18 years.
6. Capable of giving written informed consent.
7. Has not has pancreatitis within the previous 3 months.
8. Women of child-bearing potential must have a negative pregnancy test in the week before nCLE, AND be using an adequate contraception method, which must be continued for at least 1 week after nCLE.

3. Subjects for whom EUS-FNA or surgery are contraindicated

1. Treatment-naïve, Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) participants with Ann Arbor Stage 3 or 4 disease.

   Note: Participants must have histologically confirmed classical HL according to the current world health organization classification.
2. Participants must have bidimensional measurable disease as documented by radiographic technique (spiral computed tomography \[CT\] preferred) per the international working group revised criteria for response assessment for malignant lymphoma.
3. Male or female participants 18 years or older.
4. Eastern cooperative oncology group (ECOG) performance status less than or equal to (≤)2.
5. Female participants who:

   * Are postmenopausal for at least 1 year before the screening visit, OR
   * Are surgically sterile, OR
   * If they are of childbearing potential, agree to practice 1 highly effective method and 1 additional effective (barrier) method of contraception at the same time, from the time of signing of the informed consent form (ICF) through 6 months after the last dose of study drug, OR
   * Agree to practice true abstinence when this is in line with the preferred and usual lifestyle of the participant. (Periodic abstinence \[e.g., calendar, ovulation, symptothermal, post-ovulation methods\], withdrawal, spermicides only, and lactational amenorrhea are not acceptable methods of contraception. Female and male condoms should not be used together).
6. Male participants, even if surgically sterilized (i.e., status post-vasectomy), who:

   * Agree to practice effective barrier contraception during the entire study treatment period and through 6 months after the last dose of study drug, OR
   * Agree to practice true abstinence when this is in line with the preferred and usual lifestyle of the participant. (Periodic abstinence \[e.g., calendar, ovulation, symptothermal, post-ovulation methods for the female partner\], withdrawal, spermicides only, and lactational amenorrhea are not acceptable methods of contraception. Female and male condoms should not be used together).
7. Voluntary written consent must be given before performance of any study-related procedure not part of standard medical care, with the understanding that consent may be withdrawn by the participant at any time without prejudice to future medical care.
8. Clinical laboratory values as specified below within 7 days before the first dose of study drug:

   * Absolute neutrophil count greater than or equal to (≥)1,000 per microliter (1,000/μL) unless there is known HL marrow involvement
   * Platelet count ≥75,000/μL unless there is known HL marrow involvement
   * Total bilirubin must be lesser than (\<)1.5 x upper limit of the normal range (ULN) unless the elevation is known to be due to Gilbert syndrome.
   * Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) must be \<3.0 x ULN. An AST and ALT may be elevated up to 5 times the ULN if their elevation can be reasonably ascribed to the presence of HL in liver.

Note: Moderate or severe hepatic disease patients will be excluded based upon Child-Pugh criteria.

* Serum creatinine must be \<2.0 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL) and/or creatinine clearance or calculated creatinine clearance \>30 mL/minute (Cockcroft-Gault Equation).
* Hemoglobin must be ≥8 grams per deciliter (g/dL).

Exclusion Criteria

1. Female participants who are both lactating and breastfeeding or who have a positive serum pregnancy test during the screening period or a positive pregnancy test on Day 1 before first dose of study drug.
2. Any serious medical or psychiatric illness that could, in the investigator's opinion, potentially interfere with the completion of treatment according to this protocol.
3. Known cerebral or meningeal disease (HL or any other etiology), including signs or symptoms of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).
4. Symptomatic neurologic disease compromising normal activities of daily living or requiring medications.
5. Any sensory or motor peripheral neuropathy.
6. Any active systemic viral, bacterial, or fungal infection requiring systemic antibiotics within 2 weeks prior to first study drug dose.
7. Prior immunosuppressive chemotherapy, therapeutic radiation, or any immunotherapy (e.g., immunoglobulin replacement, other monoclonal antibody therapies) within 12 weeks of first study drug dose.
8. Previously treated with brentuximab vedotin.
9. Any contraindications to the concomitant chemotherapy regimens (doxorubicin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine).
10. Known hypersensitivity to recombinant proteins, murine proteins, or to any excipient contained in the drug formulation of brentuximab vedotin or any component of doxorubicin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine (AVD).
11. Known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) positive.
12. Known hepatitis B surface antigen-positive, or known or suspected active hepatitis C infection.
13. Diagnosed or treated for another malignancy within 3 years before the first dose or previously diagnosed with another malignancy and have any evidence of residual disease. Participants with nonmelanoma skin cancer or carcinoma in situ of any type are not excluded if they have undergone complete resection.
14. Any of the following cardiovascular conditions or values within 6 months before the first dose of study drug:

    1. A left-ventricular ejection fraction \<50%
    2. Myocardial infarction within 2 years of enrollment
    3. New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class 3 or 4 heart failure. The planned sample size was 306 participants. A total of 305 participants were enrolled and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive either Qingyi Huaji (QYHJ) optimized formula combined with standard treatment or a matched placebo combined with the same standard treatment.

The primary outcome was overall survival, defined as the time from randomization to death from any cause and assessed for up to 24 months. Secondary outcomes included progression-free survival, quality of life, safety, and improvement in traditional Chinese medicine symptoms. Traditional Chinese medicine syndrome classification was recorded for exploratory analyses but was not an eligibility requirement.

The hypothesis was that adding QYHJ optimized formula to standard chemotherapy would prolong overall survival without causing an unacceptable increase in toxicity. The study was conducted from April 17, 2023, through December 30, 2025.","detailedDescription":"Pancreatic cancer is a digestive tract tumor with high malignancy and poor prognosis. The overall 5-year survival rate of early stage patients after surgery is less than 9%, while the median survival time of advanced stage patients is only 3-6 months. According to statistics, in 2020, there were about 420,000 new cases of pancreatic cancer worldwide, and about 410,000 deaths. In China, with the improvement of people's living standards and the progress of population aging, the incidence of pancreatic cancer is rising year by year, ranking 7th among men, and the mortality rate is 6th among men and 8th among women.

Due to its deep anatomical location, lack of typical clinical symptoms, and easy invasion and metastasis of tumors, pancreatic cancer is difficult to be detected in the early stage. More than 80% of patients are in local advanced stage or have distant metastasis at the time of diagnosis, thus losing the opportunity for radical surgery. Currently gemcitabine combined with albumin-binding paclitaxel regimen or FOLFIRINOX (fluorouracil, calcium leucovorin, irinotecan, oxaliplatin) regimen is the first-line chemotherapy regimen for pancreatic cancer.

However, pancreatic cancer has poor sensitivity to chemical and radiotherapy, and there has been little progress in targeted therapy and immunotherapy, resulting in no significant improvement in the survival rate of pancreatic cancer in recent decades. Meanwhile, the curative effect of other common tumors has made rapid progress. It is estimated by the NCI in the United States that if there is no breakthrough in the treatment of pancreatic cancer, pancreatic cancer will become the second largest tumor killer in human by 2030.

After nearly 20 years of dedicated research, the research team of Fudan University Shanghai cancer center, has carried out the integrated treatment mode of traditional Chinese and Western medicine to improve the survival of advanced pancreatic cancer patients, making the median OS of advanced pancreatic cancer patients reach the world leading level by 45% longer than that of chemotherapy alone, and the 3-year, 5-year survival rate reaches 15% and 6.2%, respectively. However, for patients with stage IV pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, improving survival and quality of life remains an important clinical need.

The results suggest that QingyiHuayi formula has certain anti-tumor effect in advanced pancreatic cancer, and the combination of Qingyi Huayi formula with chemotherapy can prolong the survival period of patients, improve the clinical benefit rate, and may improve the therapeutic effective rate, without increasing the adverse reaction of radiotherapy and chemotherapy. The pathogenesis theory of cancer toxins puts forward that the pathogenesis of cancer toxins should be the core of syndrome differentiation, which solves the complicated and difficult problem of TCM tumor classification by disease differentiation. Four key points of clinical identification of cancer toxins pathogenesis were put forward to achieve the breakthrough of cancer virus identification and diagnosis technology bottleneck. To establish anti-cancer and detoxification treatment methods and classification of anti-cancer and detoxification Chinese medicines, and promote the clinical precision treatment and drug use of TCM tumors. Therefore, Qingyihuayi formula is a safe and effective treatment plan for advanced pancreatic cancer. After optimization, more clinical studies are needed to clarify the value of Qingyihuayi formula in the treatment of advanced pancreatic cancer and find more target groups of benefits.

In order to control random allocation and allocation hiding and ensure the science and standardization of randomized controlled trials, IWRS system of Beijing Biaoji Information Technology Co., Ltd. was used for randomization.

In order to ensure data multi-channel upload, safe storage, data desensitization and data sharing, as well as the accuracy of data entry and simple cleaning, the EDC system needs to be established. Beijing Biaozhi Information Technology Co., Ltd. is entrusted with the EDC system. It includes: ①EDC system; ②System supporting services: CRF annotation, eCRF establishment and testing, logic verification (logic verification plan, logic verification rule programming, logic verification rule testing), EDC training services; ③ Project management.

The sample-size calculation assumed a median overall survival of 4.43 months in the control group and 7.03 months in the experimental group. The test level (α) is set as 0.05, the test efficacy (1-β) as 0.80, and the expected shedding rate is 10%. After calculating by PASS software, a total of 306 patients are expected to be enrolled, and the experimental group and control group were randomly divided by 1:1, with 153 patients in the experimental group and 153 in the control group.

Descriptive statistical analysis will be used in this study. The measurement data are described by mean, standard deviation, median, lower quartile, upper quartile, minimum and maximum. 8. 11. SIRI value ≥0.8; SIRI = N × M/L, N, M, and L represent peripheral blood neutrophil, monocyte, and lymphocyte counts, respectively.

Exclusion Criteria:

4. Patients with co-infection requiring intravenous antibiotic treatment.
5. Pregnant or lactating women. Women of childbearing age who were unwilling or unable to use an acceptable method of contraception throughout the treatment period of this trial and within 12 weeks after the final administration of the study drug.
6. Known pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, acinar cell carcinoma, intraductal papillary tumors and other types of pancreatic tumors.
7. Past or concurrent cancers with a primary focus or histologically distinct from pancreatic cancer, except cervical carcinoma in situ, treated basal cell carcinoma, and superficial bladder tumors (Ta, Tis \& T1). whether the experimental drug R115777 (Tipifarnib) can shrink or slow the growth of plexiform neurofibromas in children and young adults with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and determine what side effects are related to treatment. Plexiform tumors arise from nerves; the only effective treatment is surgical removal. Often, however, not all the tumors can be removed, because of their number or location.

Patients with NF1 have a reduced amount of the protein neurofibromin. Neurofibromin is thought to help control the activity of another protein, called ras, which regulates cell growth. Too little neurofibromin, therefore, may allow for uncontrolled cell growth and tumor formation. R115777 interferes with the function of the ras and other proteins. In test tube and animal studies, R115777 has blocked the growth of cancer cells. This study will examine whether the drug is effective against plexiform tumors.

Patients with NF1 and progressive plexiform neurofibromas between 3 and 25 years of age may be eligible for this study. Patients whose tumors can be successfully removed surgically may not participate in this study. Candidates are screened with a medical history and physical and eye examinations, blood and urine tests, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Photographs are taken of tumors visible on the body surface.

Study participants are randomly assigned to receive either R115777 or placebo (an inactive substance). They take R115777 or placebo tablets every 12 hours for 21 days, followed by a 7-day rest period. This constitutes one 28-day treatment cycle. Treatment continues for as long as the tumors remain stable or shrink and side effects are tolerable. The treatment is switched (for example, from placebo to R115777) or stopped if the tumors grow or if side effects become unacceptable. Patients (or their parents) keep a record of side effects.

For the first 3 treatment cycles, patients have a physical examination and blood tests every other week. Blood tests are also done before starting treatment, and at one time point after at least 14 days of treatment to measure the effect of R115777 on proteins in blood cells. A blood sample is obtained before starting treatment and before cycles 4, 7 and 10 and then after every 6 cycles to measure the level of a substance called nerve growth factor. The analysis of nerve growth factor is used to determine if it can predict which patients might be at risk of developing side effects from R115777.","detailedDescription":"R115777 (Tipifarnib) is a farnesyltransferase inhibitor that blocks the post-translational isoprenylation of ras and other farnesylated proteins. The ras proteins are integral in cell signaling pathways, and farnesylation is essential for the function of both mutant and non-mutant ras proteins. Patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) have an increased risk of developing tumors of the central and peripheral nervous system, and there are no standard treatment options, other than surgery, available for these tumors. Neurofibromin, which is the product of the NF1 gene, contains a domain with significant homology to ras GTPase-activating proteins (GAP). Although NF1 patients lack germline ras mutations, the decreased levels of neurofibromin have been shown to be associated with a constitutively activated ras-GTP status. Thus, upstream inhibition of ras farnesylation may inhibit growth of tumors in NF1 patients. A randomized, cross-over, double-blinded, placebo-controlled pediatric phase II trial of oral R115777 will be performed in children and young adults with NF1, who have progressive, plexiform neurofibroma(s) to determine the effect of this novel anticancer drug on the rate of growth of neurofibromas. The endpoint of the trial is time to progression.
